extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy / readers of Plato's Republic
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and diagnosing forms of government (timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, tyranny) and the corresponding character-types of citizens; explains origins, defining features, defects, and psychological makeup of each regime and individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper guardian knowledge / law of births
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must know the 'law of births' and avoid unseasonable unions; ignorance in guardians about proper pairings produces unworthy children and corrupts future guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'For when your guardians are ignorant of the law of births, and unite bride and bridegroom out of season, the children will not be goodly or fortunate.' Consequence: neglect of music then gymnastics, poorer cultivation of youth, decline in testing the 'metal' of races → mixing of classes and ensuing social disorder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of discord from mixing races/metals
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing the metaphorical 'metals' (gold, silver, brass, iron) in citizens leads to inequality, dissimilarity, hatred and war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'iron will be mingled with silver, and brass with gold... which always and in all places are causes of hatred and war.' Used as an explanatory criterion for the origin of social discord when guardianship and selection fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timocracy (form of government) — defining features
rubrics_metrics.description: A State intermediate between oligarchy and aristocracy: honours rulers, warrior class abstains from agriculture/handicrafts/trade, common meals, emphasis on gymnastics and military training, fear of philosophers, preference for passionate characters fitted for war, perpetual warfare and military stratagems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text emphasizes both resemblances to the perfect State (honour to rulers, gymnastic) and peculiarities (fear of philosophers, mixed elements, warlike focus). Also notes timocracy's tendency toward covetousness: 'they will be covetous of money... hoard in dark places... castles... nests for their eggs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Timocratic individual — character profile
rubrics_metrics.description: A lover of power and honour, soldier by nature, friend of culture but less cultivated, good listener not speaker, rough with slaves, courteous to freemen, obedient to authority, lover of gymnastic and the chase; despises riches when young but becomes attracted to them with age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Origin story: often son of a brave father in an ill-governed city; social influences (mother's complaints, household talk) push him to assertiveness and ambition. Philosophy tempered with music is described as his best guardian; its absence explains his decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy (form of government) — defining feature: property qualification
rubrics_metrics.description: Government resting on a valuation of property in which the rich hold power and the poor are excluded; citizenship is tied to a fixed sum of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'They next proceed to make a law which fixes a sum of money as the qualification of citizenship... they allow no one whose property falls below the amount fixed to have any share in the government.' The degree of exclusivity varies by the sum fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchy — systemic defects
rubrics_metrics.description: Key defects include: the State effectively split into two (rich vs poor), incapability of sustained war (either must arm the multitude or be too few to fight), extremes of wealth and poverty, rise of paupers and criminals, and general inability to act as a unified polity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives examples and consequences: division fosters conspiracy and internal strife; oligarchs' unwillingness to pay taxes; paupers become a breeding-ground for thieves and malefactors; the analogy of drones in a hive is used to show the city's plague.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oligarchical individual — character profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Penurious, laborious, values wealth above other goods, satisfies only necessary appetites, shabby and thrifty, not a cultivated person; bad passions are kept down by fear of losing possessions rather than by reason, so he is internally conflicted ('two men, and not one').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'in his ordinary dealings which give him a reputation for honesty he coerces his bad passions by an enforced virtue... and the natural desires of the drone commonly exist in him all the same whenever he has to spend what is not his own.' Example: abuses in guardianship of an orphan reveal rogueries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition timocracy → oligarchy (origins of oligarchy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Accumulation of private gold and a growing love of money erode timocracy and give rise to oligarchy; rich emulate and then rival one another, favour money over virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'The accumulation of gold in the treasury of private individuals is the ruin of timocracy... one, seeing another grow rich, seeks to rival him, and thus the great mass of the citizens become lovers of money.' This social process produces laws and institutions that institutionalize wealth as political qualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition oligarchy → democracy (origins of democracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread extravagance and the ruin of good families produce large numbers of disgruntled poor who conspire or are armed and who, upon victory, grant equal freedom and power to many; magistrates often become elected by lot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text explains the social dynamics: rulers profit from spendthrift ruin; men of good family are reduced to beggary yet remain in the city eager for revolution. After the poor conquer, they grant freedom and power widely, producing democratic institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy — defining features
rubrics_metrics.description: A State characterized by freedom, frankness, and the greatest variety of human natures; equality (often indiscriminate) and a 'spangled' assortment of constitutions and ways of life; forgiving spirit and disregard for the cultivation required of true statesmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'This State... seems likely to be the fairest of States, being like an embroidered robe... a variety of colours... charming.' Also notes democratic tolerance for formerly condemned persons, and its contempt for 'fine principles' that cultivate statesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic individual — character profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Often the son of an oligarchic father who alternately suppresses and indulges desires; lives a motley, manifold life, treating all pleasures as equally good, shifting capriciously between pursuits (drink, gymnastics, philosophy, politics), and prizes liberty and equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text details the psychological development: initial suppression of unnecessary desires, subsequent indulgence under bad influences, and eventual balance or chaotic alternation among pleasures: 'his life has neither law nor order... he lives from day to day indulging the appetite of the hour.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary vs unnecessary pleasures — classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary pleasures are those essential to health and life and beneficial (e.g., simple food for strength); unnecessary pleasures are those we could do without, often harmful to body and soul and impediments to wisdom and virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: defines the two classes and gives examples (simple food, condiments as necessary only insofar as they are healthy; delicacies and luxury as unnecessary). This distinction is used to evaluate individuals' moral characters and regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy's excess of freedom can produce tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive thirst for freedom and the neglect of other goods in a democracy can lead to its dissolution and create conditions in which tyranny arises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: 'When a democracy which is thirsting for freedom has evil cup-bearers presiding over the feast... she calls [rulers] to account... and this leads to a demand for tyranny.' The metaphor of being 'drunk of freedom' is used to show how excess leads to instability and desire for a single ruler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honouring wealth over virtue undermines the State
rubrics_metrics.description: When society and laws honour wealth more than virtue, virtue is dishonoured and neglected; as riches are prized, the civic esteem for the virtuous declines and social goods are reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text states: 'when riches and virtue are placed together in the scales of the balance, the one always rises as the other falls.' This principle explains moral and political degeneration across regime transitions.
